title: Lantern Night
subtitle: Friday 16 September 1977: The Closing Party, the Mask Box, and the Last Lanterns on the Water

setting.name: Camp Pinecrest, the Lodge, the Playhouse and the swimming dock, Friday 16 September 1977
setting.description: The party's first evening at Pinecrest. Nothing is hostile yet and nobody is hurt. The old staff are glad to see each other, the Lodge smells of woodsmoke and Winnie's baking, and the closing weekend has the bittersweet, slightly drunk warmth of a last reunion. The point of this scenario is to make Pinecrest a real place full of people the players like, to bring the pregens together, to put the masks and the lake in front of them, and to let the first wrong things happen on the water. It ends just before midnight, with the rain beginning and a man the party has just been drinking with standing on the dock where he cannot be.
setting.atmosphere: Golden afternoon, then a long blue dusk, then the lake going black and still. Make the people vivid and the place a little sad: peeling paint, a stack of mattresses in the Playhouse wings, a SOLD sign leaning against the gatehouse, laughter that goes on a beat too long. The wrongness is all at the edges and all about faces: the photo wall, the masks, the lanterns' light on the water, a reflection that does not move when its owner does. Coach is the warmest man in the Mountains and never once goes near the water.

keyLocations.name: The Lodge
keyLocations.description: The ice company's stone bunkhouse of 1881, rebuilt in 1934: a long grey building with a deep porch facing the lake, a lounge with a stone fireplace big enough to stand in, an upright piano, a color television on a rolling stand, a bar in the corner with a hand-lettered sign (HONOR SYSTEM, 50¢), and twelve guest rooms upstairs with iron bedsteads and lake views. Every doorway, front, back and upstairs, has a worn iron sill plate set into the floor, a relic of the ice company that nobody has ever bothered to take up.
features: The iron sill plates in every doorway, worn smooth and bright down the middle by ninety years of boots; the guest cabins on Birch Row have plain wooden sills
The lounge windows: eight tall panes facing the lake; after dark, with the lamps lit, they are black mirrors
The Honor System bar: rye, gin, Rolling Rock in a cooler, a cigar box of quarters
A framed 1934 brochure by the door: CAMP PINECREST ON LANTERN LAKE — A SUMMER CAMP FOR GROWN-UPS — FOR BUSINESS MEN AND WOMEN OF EIGHTEEN YEARS AND OVER — $22.50 THE WEEK
encounters: Marvin Eckhart at the piano, all evening, taking requests
Gene Marcotte and Santi Rivera, the developer's survey crew, at the bar after supper
Bev Kleinfelter, telling anyone who will listen about the man on the dock on Thursday night
secrets: The iron sills will matter on Saturday night: Old Glass cannot cross them unless the person whose face it wears invites it in (Old Glass: Its Rules, Rule Three). Nobody alive knows this but Alvin, and Coach.

CLUE D1 (core): nobody can remember Coach saying his own name. Ask Opal directly (Insight DC 12 to see it hit her): "He hasn't said it in fifteen years. He says it's a camp thing. Coach is Coach." He introduces himself to every new arrival as "Coach, just Coach, friend", and he signs the guest book C.S.

keyLocations.name: The Dining Hall and the Photo Wall
keyLocations.description: A long timber hall joined to the Lodge by a covered walk: eight long tables with oilcloth, a kitchen behind a swinging door, a bell on the porch. Along the north wall hang forty-three framed staff photographs, one for every season from 1934 to 1976, rows of young adults in white shirts and sneakers squinting into the sun on the Lodge steps, each frame with a typed label.
features: 1934: Philomena Delamater in the centre, a small woman in a cloche hat; beside her a big man in a cap, RUDOLPH DREHER, CARETAKER
1946 to 1976: Alvin Dreher at the end of every back row, getting greyer
1955 to 1962: CURTIS SEELEY, WATERFRONT, broad-shouldered and grinning, a whistle on a lanyard; in 1962 Nell Sorensen (Drama) and Odessa Grimes (Nurse) are in the same row
1965 to 1976: 'COACH' SEELEY, DIRECTOR, front and centre every year, and in every one of the twelve photographs his face is a soft grey smear, as if he moved; the faces on either side are sharp
Winnie Szot in every photograph from 1946, in an apron
encounters: Winnie Szot, in the kitchen from four o'clock, rolling pastry
Supper at 6:30 for everyone on the Neck: twenty-two people at three tables
secrets: CLUE D2 (core, automatic for anyone who looks along the wall): twelve photographs in a row, 1965 to 1976, and Coach is a blur in every one. Opal says what everyone says: "He can't stand still for a picture. Never could." Investigation DC 12: the shutter speeds were the same; nobody else in twelve years blurred. A fear check against the sign of it (DC 10) for anyone who looks hard and thinks about it.

Compare 1962 and 1965 (Perception DC 13): Curtis in 1962 is standing with his weight on one hip, laughing, sleeves rolled; Coach in 1965 stands like a man waiting to be told he can sit, hands clasped at his belt, the way men stood for photographs before the First War.

There is no 1963 or 1964 photograph. The camp was under Herbert Amsel's management those years; Opal says "they stopped doing them for a while, after that summer". Which summer? "1962. Somebody drowned. Well, nobody drowned. Curtis's canoe got loose. It was a bad weekend."

keyLocations.name: The Playhouse
keyLocations.description: A white clapboard theatre of 1938 with two hundred folding seats, a raked stage, a velvet curtain the moths have been at, and a projection booth. For thirty-nine summers it held the Saturday revue: skits, songs, a chorus line of stenographers and a comic who sold insurance the other fifty-one weeks of the year. Tonight Bev Kleinfelter is running her slide carousel of forty years of Pinecrest and Marvin is at the upright in the pit.
features: Bev's Kodak carousel: eighty slides, 1938 to 1976, canoes, tennis whites, costume nights, Lantern Nights with rows of carved masks lit from below
The wings: stacked mattresses, flats from a 1959 production of a musical about sailors, a box of dusty costume masks of the theatrical kind, papier-mâché, which are not the Lantern Night masks
The playbill wall in the lobby, every revue since 1938, with Nell Sorensen's name on the 1961 and 1962 bills
encounters: The slide show at 7:30: forty minutes, Bev narrating, Marvin playing, the old staff calling out names
Nell Sorensen, if she is played, recognised and applauded; if she is not, Bev mentions "our Nell, who's on the stage now, in Atlantic City"
secrets: Bev skips one slide. Perception DC 12 to notice the click and the hurry; if asked, she goes back to it: Lantern Night 1962, the dock, no masks, a row of young faces lit from below by lanterns, and at the end of the dock Curtis Seeley leaning over the water, looking down. "Mr. Amsel didn't like the masks. That was the year we didn't." Coach, at the back of the hall, has already left.

Lantern Night slides from 1938 to 1961 (Investigation DC 10 to notice): every face on the dock is masked, staff and guests alike; the masks come off only on the beach. Several slides show Alvin, or before him Rudolph, standing at the dock's foot with the cedar box like a man taking tickets.

keyLocations.name: The Swimming Dock
keyLocations.description: An L of grey planks running a hundred feet straight out from the beach and fifty feet across at the end, with a ladder at the corner, a diving board long since removed, and iron lantern posts every ten feet with hooks for the paper lanterns. At night, with no wind, the water around it is so still it looks solid.
features: The iron lantern posts, made by the ice company as channel markers and set into the dock in 1934
A wooden crate of sixty paper lanterns on cedar shingles, each with a stub of candle, and a box of kitchen matches
A brass plaque at the dock's foot: LANTERN NIGHT — LEAVE YOUR FACE AT HOME, TAKE YOUR LANTERN WITH YOU — P.D. 1934
encounters: Lantern Night at 9 p.m.: everyone on the Neck except Coach, Alvin and Winnie (who watches from the Dining Hall porch, as she has every year)
The man in the mask on the dam spillway at about 9:40
secrets: Old Glass rises tonight, at Gene's lantern, and from then on it sees every face that looks into the water or out of a lakeside window after dark (Old Glass: Its Rules, Rule One). Note which characters look into the water and for how long; any of them can be borrowed from Saturday night on.
CLUE B1 (core, 11:45 p.m.): see Act 3, Two Genes.

The plaque's motto is Philomena's joke on the rule she was given. Occult DC 13, or Zachary's Folklorist interview: masks at a water festival are found in a dozen folk customs, and the usual reason given is so that whatever is in the water cannot see you.

keyLocations.name: The Boathouse and the Dock Path
keyLocations.description: A long shingled building on pilings at the waterline, west of the dock, with canoes racked three high, four rowboats, the ice company's flat-bottomed workboat, a workshop at the back with a vise and a wall of tools, and a covered slip under the floor where black water slaps quietly against the pilings. The path from the Lodge to the dock runs past its door.
features: The covered slip: a square of black water eight feet across under a hinged hatch; colder than the lake
The workshop: Coach's Suburban's service records on a clipboard, oil cans, and in a drawer a box of spare spark plugs
A rack of ice tools on the back wall, kept for history: saws, tongs, a breaking bar, and six long ice pikes on pegs
encounters: Alvin Dreher on the dock path at 8:45 with the cedar mask box (Act 2, The Mask Box)
Coach, who spends the evening here "fixing a canoe rib" and watching the dock through the workshop window
secrets: CLUE D5 (Perception DC 13 if anyone watches Coach handle the ice pikes while he tidies the rack): he takes one down and holds it the way only a man who has cut ice holds it, hands apart, weight back, and then hangs it up as if it were hot. Ask him and he laughs: "History, pal. Rudolph showed me once."
Tonight there are six ice pikes on the rack. By morning there will be five (CLUE A3).
The slip is where Old Glass will lie by day, from Saturday on. Tonight it is only cold water. Anyone with The Thin Place who stands over the hatch feels longing, like someone waiting at a window.

synopsis: Friday afternoon the party arrives at Camp Pinecrest for its closing weekend: a reunion of the old staff, a supper, a slide show, and one last Lantern Night on the dock before the camp is sold on Monday. They meet Coach, the booming, kindly director; his sister Opal, who runs the office; Winnie Szot, who has cooked here since 1946; the developer's survey crew, Gene Marcotte and Santi Rivera; and the old staff. Officer Nolan Pomeroy takes Bev Kleinfelter's statement about a masked man on the dock on Thursday night. At supper the photo wall shows something wrong with Coach's face. At 8:45 the caretaker, Alvin Dreher, comes down the dock path with a cedar box of carved masks for Lantern Night and Coach sends him away in front of everyone; one mask is missing when the box is put back. At nine, without masks, the old staff set their lanterns on the water, Coach invites Gene to light the first one and look a good long while, and the lake looks back. A reflection does not move when its owner does. A man in a carved mask watches from the dam. At 11:45, as the rain begins, someone at the Lodge window sees Gene Marcotte standing at the end of the dock in the rain, staring at the Lodge, while Gene is sitting at the bar behind them.
hook: Each pregen's sheet gives a reason to be on the Neck this afternoon. Opal Seeley wrote to Nell Sorensen and Odessa Grimes, both on the 1962 staff, asking them back for the closing. Paula Hixon's editor wants a feature on the last grown-ups' camp in the Poconos. Zachary Fenstermacher has Opal's permission to look at the ice company's papers in the Office attic. Victor Zelinsky starts as Ridgeview's off-season watchman on Monday and has come up with Gene to see the place. Nolan Pomeroy is here because Opal called the township this morning about the man in the mask. Roscoe Talmadge, the game protector, is here about a bear in the Dining Hall's garbage, and Winnie has asked him to stay for pie.

clues: D1: he never says his own name, and Opal has not heard it from him in fifteen years
D2: his face is blurred in all twelve staff photographs since 1965
D5: the champion swimmer will not set foot on the dock, and holds an ice pike like a cutter
E1: he sent the masks away and asked a stranger to look into the water

conclusions.conclusion: The masks were never a costume
clues: A1: Alvin's insistence, and his words to whoever takes a mask: 'Wear it on the water. Don't look down.'
C1: the plaque's motto, 'Leave your face at home', and Bev's slides of every Lantern Night masked until 1962
C1: Winnie: 'Miss Delamater said the lake mustn't see you. I thought it was poetry.'
Zachary's folklore: masks at the water so the thing in it cannot see you

conclusions.conclusion: Somebody is in two places at once
clues: The reflection that did not move, on the dock at Lantern Night
B1: 'Gene' on the dock at 11:45 while Gene sits at the bar
B5: Paula's Polaroid of the dock, which shows a grey shape with no face beside the ladder (develops tonight; its meaning lands in pc-scenario-002)

acts.title: Friday Afternoon: Arrival
acts.description: The party arrives between three and five, meets each other and the camp, and sits down to supper. Nobody is hostile and nothing frightening happens yet. The purpose of this act is to make Pinecrest a place the players are sorry to see sold, to give each pregen a person to care about, and to plant the photo wall, Coach's name and the masked man on Thursday night.
objectives: Meet Coach, Opal and Winnie, and get a room in the Lodge or a cabin on Birch Row
Take Bev Kleinfelter's statement about the man in the mask (Nolan, or anyone)
Eat supper at the long tables and meet the other guests

scenes.name: The Gravel Lot
scenes.description: Between three and five the cars come in: Gene's Ridgeview pickup with Santi and Victor, Nolan's township Fury, Paula's Beetle, Odessa's Buick, Zachary on the bus to Larkin Corners and a lift from Roscoe in the Game Commission truck, Nell in a rented Pinto. Opal meets each arrival with her clipboard: rooms in the Lodge for the old staff and the women who ask, cabins on Birch Row for everyone else ("they're cosy, they've got screens, the blankets are in the trunk at the foot of the bed"). Coach comes up from the Boathouse with his arms out, a big brown man in a cardigan with a whistle on a lanyard, and greets everyone as 'friend', 'pal' or 'Doctor', shaking hands with both of his. He knows Nell and Odessa at once and hugs them, and says how glad he is, and calls them by name; he never says his own. The players should meet each other here and on the porch: let them talk.
scenes.readAloud: The road comes out of the hemlocks onto a gravel lot above the water, and there it is: a long grey stone lodge with a porch, a dining hall, a white wooden theatre, a row of little green cabins along the shore, and a dock running out into a lake so still that the far hills stand upside down in it, every tree. A banner on the porch says THANK YOU PINECREST 1934–1977. Somebody inside is playing the piano. A woman with a clipboard and reading glasses on a chain is already coming up the path. Behind her, from the boathouse, a big man in a cardigan comes up the slope with his arms spread wide and a whistle bouncing on his chest, calling out, "There they are! Welcome, welcome, friends. Welcome home." He shakes your hand with both of his. His hands are warm and very strong, and calloused across the palms in a way that does not quite go with the cardigan.

skillChecks.success: Coach's welcome is real, and so is something under it: he is tired in a way that has nothing to do with the drive, and every time he glances at the lake he looks away a little too fast. He has looked at the water from the corner of his eye four times and not once straight on.
skillChecks.failure: Coach is the kind of man who makes a place. You can see why people came back for thirty years.

skillChecks.success: A SOLD sign is leaning against the gatehouse wall, face in, as if someone could not stand to look at it. And from the porch you can see every building on the Neck except one: the low stone shape of the old Icehouse by the dam, which has no windows at all.
skillChecks.failure: It is a lovely, shabby, well-kept place. The paint is peeling. The grass is cut.

scenes.name: Bev's Statement
scenes.description: Bev Kleinfelter, 55, arts and crafts counselor from 1949 to 1971, arrived Thursday afternoon to help Opal with the decorations. Nolan Pomeroy has come to take her statement, and anyone can sit in. Thursday at about 10:30 p.m. she walked down to the beach to see the stars and saw a man standing at the end of the dock in a mask, a carved one, "one of ours, from Lantern Night, I'd know them anywhere", looking down into the water with a lantern held out over it at arm's length, but with its shutter closed. She called "Hello?" He turned his head and looked at her, didn't answer, and walked off the end of the dock along the stringer to the shore, quick and sure in the dark, and was gone into the trees toward the dam. She was frightened and is embarrassed to have been. "It was probably Alvin. He's peculiar about the lake. But he's never once in thirty years not said good evening to me."
scenes.readAloud: Bev Kleinfelter is a small, brisk woman with silver hair in a braid and paint under her fingernails, and she tells it twice, once fast and once slowly. "A mask. One of the Lantern Night ones, the carved ones, Miss Delamater's. I'd know them anywhere, I repainted them all in 1958. He had a lantern held right out over the water, at the end of the dock, like this, at arm's length, but it was shut. Dark. Like he wanted to see down into the water without — " She stops. "Without the water seeing the light? That's silly. I'm sorry. I called hello and he just looked at me. Then he walked off along the side of the dock, in the dark, on that little beam, like a cat. I didn't sleep."

skillChecks.success: Bev's account is precise and consistent. The man walked away toward the dam, which means toward the caretaker's cottage and the Icehouse, not toward the road. Whoever he was, he knew the dock stringer well enough to walk it in the dark, and he was not trying to hurt anyone; he was looking at the water.
skillChecks.failure: A prowler in a costume mask, at a closing camp, on a Thursday night. It happens.

skillChecks.success: She is not making it up, and she is not mainly frightened of the man. She is frightened of the way he held the lantern. She has seen someone do that before, a long time ago, and she does not want to remember where.
skillChecks.failure: She is upset, and a little embarrassed, and glad of the company.

scenes.name: Supper at the Long Tables
scenes.description: At 6:30 Winnie rings the porch bell and twenty-two people sit down at three long tables: chicken pot pie, the Pennsylvania kind with square noodles, creamed corn, pepper cabbage, rolls, and three kinds of pie. Coach says a few words, the old staff toast Pinecrest and Miss Delamater, and Marvin Eckhart is persuaded to sing. Seat the pregens together. At the next table Gene Marcotte, the developer's surveyor, a pleasant, balding man with a bad back, is telling Victor and Santi about the plan for the Neck ("they'll take the lake down eight feet for a beach, put a clubhouse where the Playhouse is"), and gets some hard looks from the old staff. Santi Rivera, his young rodman, says little and eats like a man who has been in the Army. Roscoe Talmadge eats three slices of Winnie's apple crumb pie and tells everyone the bear is a two-year-old boar who will be fine if they keep the cans closed. Winnie comes out of the kitchen to sit for five minutes with Odessa and Nell, whom she has missed. Opal mentions that her brother "hasn't been in the lake in fifteen years, if you can believe it, the man who swam it end to end. His shoulder."
scenes.readAloud: The dining hall is warm and loud and smells of chicken and pastry. Forty-three summers of young men and women in white look down from the frames along the wall. A big woman in a flowered apron comes through the swinging door with a pie in each hand and sets them down in front of you, and puts a hand on your shoulder, and says, "You're thin. Eat." At the head of the table the big man in the cardigan stands up, taps his glass, and says, "Friends. Forty-three years. Miss Delamater bought this place for eleven thousand dollars and a promise, and every one of you kept it." He raises his glass. Everyone does. Through the windows behind him the lake has gone the color of steel, and very still.

skillChecks.success: Winnie, sitting with you for her five minutes, talks about Miss Delamater: 'A little woman, a store lady from Philadelphia, but tough. She had rules. Masks on the water. No swimming after dark. Lanterns out by midnight. She told me the lake mustn't see your face. I thought it was poetry.' (CLUE C1.)
skillChecks.failure: Winnie talks about pie, and the old days, and how she is going to her sister's in Hazleton on Tuesday and does not know what she will do with her hands.

skillChecks.success: Opal watches her brother the way a nurse watches a patient. Whenever he speaks, her mouth moves a little, as if she were waiting for a word. When he finishes his toast without saying his own name, her shoulders drop, very slightly, the way they would after a disappointment she is used to.
skillChecks.failure: Opal is busy, efficient and a little sad. It is her last weekend too.

encounters: None hostile. If anyone goes looking for Alvin Dreher this afternoon, his cottage by the dam is locked and his truck is gone (it is behind the Icehouse); a hand-lettered card on his door reads AT WORK — A.V.

acts.title: Friday Evening: The Old Staff
acts.description: From 7:30 to 9:00 the reunion has its slide show in the Playhouse, and then everyone walks down to the dock for Lantern Night. On the way, the caretaker arrives with the masks and is sent away. The purpose of this act is to put the masks in the players' hands, to show Coach deliberately leaving them off, and to let the players see who Alvin is before he becomes the man in the mask.
objectives: Watch the slide show and notice the skipped slide from 1962
Meet Alvin Dreher and the cedar mask box
Take a mask, or decide not to
Notice that Coach chooses Gene to light the first lantern, and does not come onto the dock

scenes.name: Forty Years in Eighty Slides
scenes.description: Bev's slide show in the Playhouse, Marvin at the piano playing the song that goes with each year. Canoe races, tennis whites, a 1941 costume night, a chorus line of typists in sailor suits, Lantern Nights with rows of carved masks lit from below like a congregation of strange saints. The old staff call out names and laugh. At the 1962 slide Bev clicks through fast (Perception DC 12) and goes back only if asked: the dock, no masks, and Curtis Seeley at the end of it, leaning over the water with his lantern, looking down. Coach, who was standing at the back, is gone. Marvin plays one song from 1958, a slow one called 'Lantern Lake Waltz' that he wrote for the revue that year, and Opal gets up and goes out. (Old Glass will remember this song: controlFile.oldGlass.)
scenes.readAloud: The projector hums, the slides click, and forty years go by on a bedsheet screen: women in bathing caps, men in white flannels, a canoe tipping over and everyone in the hall groaning as if it had just happened. Then a night. Rows of people on the dock with paper lanterns, and every one of them in a carved wooden face, pale, smiling a little, with a lantern painted on its brow. The lanterns are lit from below and the masks seem to float. The old staff go quiet. Somebody says, softly, "God, I'd forgotten." Click. Another year, another row of masks. Click. Click. And then, too fast, a slide with no masks at all, young faces lit gold, and at the end of the dock a big man leaning out over the black water. Click. Tennis.

skillChecks.success: You catch the skipped slide, and the man leaning over the water, and Bev's thumb on the button, quick, as if it were hot. When you look back for Coach, the door at the back of the hall is just swinging shut.
skillChecks.failure: Tennis, canoes, a costume night. The slides go by.

skillChecks.success: Masks at the water. The lanterns, the night, the last night of the season: it is a closing rite, and folk customs like it, in a dozen countries, all give the same reason for the masks. So that what lives in the water does not see who you are. (CLUE C1.)
skillChecks.failure: It is a lovely custom. Somebody should have filmed it.

scenes.name: The Mask Box
scenes.description: At 8:45, as the reunion comes down the path from the Playhouse to the dock in the dusk, Alvin Dreher is waiting at the dock's foot with a long cedar box under one arm, the way he has every Lantern Night since 1946. He is a big, grey, weather-cut man in a wool shirt, and he speaks quietly to each person as they come: "Your mask, ma'am. Mister." The box holds forty carved basswood half-faces, each with a lantern painted on its brow. Coach comes down from the Boathouse fast and says, pleasantly, in front of everyone, "Not this year, Alvin. The Ridgeview people want faces for the brochure. Put them away, pal." Alvin looks at him a long moment. Then he closes the box and walks off toward the dam. On the way he passes whichever pregen looks most likely to listen (Zachary, Nell or Odessa by preference) and pushes a mask into their hands: "Wear it on the water. Don't look down." Later the box is found on the Boathouse workbench; one mask, the oldest, Philomena's own with the lantern in gold leaf, is missing (CLUE A1).
scenes.readAloud: At the foot of the dock, in the last of the light, a big grey-haired man in a wool shirt stands with a long cedar box open in his arms like a tray. Inside, nested in straw, are carved wooden faces, pale and smooth, eyes cut out, a little lantern painted on every brow. He holds one out to the first person down the path. "Your mask, ma'am." Then the big man in the cardigan is there, smiling, a hand on his shoulder. "Not this year, Alvin. The developer's people want faces. Put them away, pal." For a moment nobody moves. The caretaker looks at the director as if he were reading something written very small. Then he shuts the lid, and walks away up the shore toward the dam. As he passes you he stops, and puts one of the masks into your hands, and says, low, not unkindly, "Wear it on the water. Don't look down."

skillChecks.success: That was not a quarrel between a boss and an employee. That was two men who have known something together for a long time, and one of them just broke a promise to the other in public. Alvin is not angry. He is frightened.
skillChecks.failure: An old caretaker who likes the old ways, and a director with a sale to close.

skillChecks.success: The mask in your hands is basswood, old, beautifully carved, worn smooth inside where a hundred faces have rested. Inked inside the brow, in a 1930s hand: PINECREST — LANTERN NIGHT — SO THE LAKE KEEPS NO FACES. P.D.
skillChecks.failure: It is an old carved mask, lighter than it looks, with a painted lantern on its brow.

scenes.name: The First Lantern
scenes.description: Coach does not come onto the dock. He stands at its foot by the plaque with a lit lantern in his hand, and when everyone is out on the L he calls Gene Marcotte back, gives him the lantern, and says, "Our guest of honour. You light the first one, friend, and set her on the water, and take a good long look. That's the custom. You look at the lake and the lake looks at you." Gene, a little embarrassed and a little drunk, does it: kneels at the corner by the ladder, sets the first lantern afloat, and looks down into the water a long while, smiling. Then the others light theirs from his and set them out. Coach goes back to the Boathouse. Anyone who asks the old staff whether that is the custom gets a puzzled "No? Miss Delamater lit the first one. Then Coach." (CLUE E1.)
scenes.readAloud: The director does not set foot on the dock. He stands at the foot of it, by the brass plaque, holding a lit paper lantern on a cedar shingle, and calls the surveyor back to him, and puts it in his hands. "Guest of honour. You light the first one, friend. Set her on the water and take a good long look. You look at the lake, and the lake looks at you." Everyone laughs. The surveyor walks out to the end of the dock with the lantern held in front of him, kneels by the ladder, and sets it down on the black water, and leans out over it, smiling, looking down at his own face in the light. He looks for a long time.

skillChecks.success: Coach is watching Gene look into the water the way a man at a track watches a horse he has bet the house on. When Gene finally stands up, Coach lets out a breath, and turns away, and walks back to the boathouse without a word to anybody.
skillChecks.failure: Coach is being a gracious host to the man who is buying his camp. It must be hard for him.

skillChecks.success: Bev or Marvin, asked: 'That's not the custom. Miss Delamater lit the first one, and then Coach, every year. And she never let anybody look at the water like that. 'Lanterns down, eyes up,' she used to say.' (CLUE E1.)
skillChecks.failure: It is a nice gesture, under the circumstances.

encounters: None hostile. Alvin will not talk tonight; followed, he walks to his cottage, goes in, and does not answer the door. If someone forces the issue he says only: "Ask him why he wants their faces. Ask him why he won't come on the dock." and shuts the door.

acts.title: Friday Night: The Lanterns
acts.description: From nine to midnight: Lantern Night on the dock, the masked man on the spillway, the rain beginning, and the double. This is the act where the lake looks back. Ask each player, as they set their lantern on the water, whether their character looks down into it, and for how long, and whether they are wearing a mask. Old Glass is up from Gene's lantern on (Old Glass: Its Rules, Rule One), and every unmasked face that looks into the lake tonight is one it can borrow.
objectives: Set the lanterns on the water, and decide whether to look
See something wrong in the water
See the man in the mask on the dam

scenes.name: Sixty Lanterns
scenes.description: Sixty paper lanterns drift slowly out from the dock across the black water, and the reunion stands along the rail with drinks in their hands, very quiet. The reflections are perfect. Anyone who looks down into the water unmasked for more than a moment sees their own face in the lantern light, and, on a Perception check DC 14 (or automatically for a Sensitive, who feels a presence below the dock the moment Gene's lantern touches the water), sees the reflection be a beat late: they turn their head, and the face in the water finishes looking at them first. Fear check, the sign of it, DC 10. Paula, or anyone with a camera, can take pictures: Polaroids of the dock and the lanterns. One Polaroid of the corner by the ladder, when it develops a minute later, shows the lanterns, the water and the dock, and Gene kneeling, and beside him, standing on the ladder up to its waist in the lake, a grey man-shape with no face (CLUE B5; the truth of it, DC 20, but only if someone looks closely; in this light it looks like a smudge on the film, and Coach, if shown, says 'Bad pack, pal, they do that').
scenes.readAloud: The lanterns drift away from the dock one by one, carried by nothing, and the water holds every one of them twice: the little paper lamp and its upside-down twin. Nobody talks. Somebody's glass clinks on the rail. You lean out to watch your own lantern go, and there you are on the black water, lit gold from below, looking up. You turn your head to say something to the person beside you. And in the corner of your eye, your face on the water is still looking at you. Then it turns, too, a moment late, and is only a reflection.

skillChecks.success: The reflection was late. Not much: a blink. But you watched it finish looking at you. Fear check, the sign of it (DC 10). And now that you look, the water under the dock is colder than the air; your breath fogs when you lean close to it, and nobody else's does.
skillChecks.failure: The lanterns, the stars, the still water. It is one of the most beautiful things you have ever seen.

skillChecks.success: A double seen in water by night is a fetch in half a dozen countries' stories: seeing your own is bad luck, worse than bad luck. But the old stories agree on one comfort. A fetch cannot say the name of the one it copies. (A clue toward Rule Two.)
skillChecks.failure: There are a hundred lake stories. This is a lovely lake.

scenes.name: The Man on the Spillway
scenes.description: At about 9:40, someone on the dock (the first player to say they look around rather than down) sees him: across the water to the south, on the lip of the dam where the lake slides over the spillway, a figure standing in the lantern light from the drifting lamps, in a pale carved mask with a lantern on its brow, holding a long pole, perfectly still, watching the dock. Fear check DC 13 (the man in the mask, an ordinary terror). If anyone shouts or points, he turns and walks off along the top of the dam into the dark. Chasing him takes three minutes along the shore path in the dark, and finds only wet stones and his boot prints going toward the Icehouse and the cottage. Roscoe Talmadge, if he follows, can say (Survival DC 12) that the prints are a big man in work boots who knew exactly where he was putting his feet, and that he stopped once and stood a long while looking back at the dock. The pole is an ice pike.
scenes.readAloud: Across the water, where the lake runs smooth and black over the lip of the old dam, someone is standing. A man, tall, in dark clothes, in the faint gold light of the drifting lanterns, with something long held upright beside him like a staff. His face is white and smooth and smiling very slightly, and there is a little lantern painted on his brow. He is not moving. He is watching the dock. Watching you. Then, as someone beside you draws a breath to shout, he turns and walks away along the top of the dam, unhurried, and the dark takes him.

skillChecks.success: The prints go along the dam and down toward the caretaker's cottage and the Icehouse. Big man, work boots, sure-footed in the dark. He stood for a long time on the dam, rocking from foot to foot as if cold. And at the end of the dam there is a mark in the mud where he set the butt of his pole: an iron point, square and deep.
skillChecks.failure: Wet stones, dark woods, the noise of the spillway. He is gone.

skillChecks.success: Whoever that was, he was not watching the party. He was watching the water under the dock, and the people leaning over it, and when Gene stood up he took a step forward, as if to shout a warning, and stopped himself.
skillChecks.failure: A man in a mask watching a party of strangers in the dark. It is exactly as frightening as it sounds.

scenes.name: Two Genes
scenes.description: By 10:30 the lanterns have gone out one by one on the water, the reunion has moved up to the Lodge, and the rain begins: a few heavy drops, then a steady downpour drumming on the porch roof. Marvin is playing; the Honor System bar is doing good business; Gene Marcotte is on a stool at the bar telling Victor and Santi about his bad back. At 11:45, someone standing at the lounge windows (choose a player character, preferably Nell; the windows are black mirrors with the lamps lit, and they have to cup their hands to see out) sees, through the rain, a man standing at the very end of the dock, in the light from the Lodge porch, bareheaded, soaked, his hands in his pockets, looking up at the Lodge. It is Gene. Gene is sitting at the bar behind them, laughing; they can see him reflected in the same window, next to the man on the dock. Fear check, seeing it, DC 15 (+2 for the dark). If they say anything aloud, or go out, the figure on the dock turns and steps off the end into the water without a splash and is gone. Gene, told, laughs, then does not, and goes out to the porch to look. Nell, if she is there, goes white: on Lantern Night 1962 she saw Curtis Seeley standing on the dock in the rain at midnight while Curtis was out on the lake in his canoe, and she left in the morning and never came back. End the scenario on the rain, the empty dock and the porch light, and Gene standing at the rail saying, "That's a hell of a joke. Who's the joker?"
scenes.readAloud: The windows of the lounge are black with the lamps lit, and you have to cup your hands against the glass to see out. Rain, sheeting across the porch light. The beach. The dock running out into the dark. And at the very end of it, standing in the rain with his hands in his pockets, bareheaded and soaked through, a man looking up at the Lodge. Looking at the window. At you. It is the surveyor, Gene. You know his bald spot, his jacket, the way he stands to favour his back. Behind you, at the bar, someone laughs, and in the black glass in front of you, next to the man on the dock, you can see the reflection of the room behind you: the fire, the piano, and Gene Marcotte on a bar stool with a beer in his hand, laughing at his own joke.

skillChecks.success: The man on the dock is not wearing a coat in the rain, and the rain does not seem to bother him. When he turns, he does not walk off the end of the dock so much as go down, straight down, like a man on a stair, and the water closes over him without a ring.
skillChecks.failure: Rain, the dark, the porch light, and then nobody at all on the end of the dock.

skillChecks.success: Nell, beside you, has seen this before. Her hand is on the glass and she is saying something under her breath, a name, over and over. 'Curtis. Curtis. Curtis.'
skillChecks.failure: Everyone has had a lot to drink. Everyone is tired.

encounters: None hostile tonight. Old Glass will not come ashore while the reunion is up and the porch is lit, and Alvin stays away from the Lodge. If a party goes out onto the dock after 11:45, they find wet footprints on the dry planks under the porch-light overhang coming up the ladder from the water, ten paces toward the shore, and stopping, and the ladder's rungs cold as January (fear check, sign, DC 10).

If anyone goes to the Boathouse after midnight, Alvin is there in the dark in the mask, at the open slip hatch with a hand mirror, and he steps out of the shadows, looks at them, holds the mirror up to their face, lowers it, and walks out the far door without a word (fear check DC 13). He has just taken the sixth ice pike from the rack.

npcsInvolved.name: 'Coach' Seeley, 45
npcsInvolved.role: Owner and director of Camp Pinecrest; host of the closing weekend
npcsInvolved.description: Big, sun-browned, booming, in a cardigan with a whistle on a lanyard he never blows; calls everyone friend or pal; never says his own name; never sets foot on the dock; calloused hands. Truly Lorenz Garside, an ice cutter born in 1886, living Curtis Seeley's life since 1962 (controlFile.suspects).
npcsInvolved.motivation: To get through Monday and away, and to give the thing in the lake somebody else's face before he goes, so that it stops looking for its own.

npcsInvolved.name: Opal Seeley, 41
npcsInvolved.role: Camp bookkeeper and office manager since 1958; Coach's sister (a companion)
npcsInvolved.description: Reading glasses on a chain, a clipboard, a cardigan, a dry wit, and a habit of watching her brother as if waiting for a word.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To close Pinecrest decently, to see the old staff once more, and, though she would not say it, to find out at last what happened to her brother in 1962.

npcsInvolved.name: Winifred "Winnie" Szot, 63
npcsInvolved.description: Big, flowered apron, flour to the elbows, a widow from Hazleton, the camp's heart. Knew Philomena Delamater and Rudolph Dreher, and has fed Alvin Dreher supper three nights a week for thirty-one years.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To feed everyone one more time, and to keep Alvin out of trouble.

npcsInvolved.name: Alvin Dreher, 58
npcsInvolved.role: Caretaker since 1946; the man in the mask
npcsInvolved.description: Big, grey, quiet, weather-cut, wool shirt, a war veteran; tonight with the cedar mask box, and later in Philomena's mask with an ice pike.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep the lake from taking anyone else, and to keep anything that it takes from crossing the Outlet.

npcsInvolved.name: Gene Marcotte, 38
npcsInvolved.description: Pleasant, balding, a bad back, a wife in Emmaus, a laugh you can hear across a room; a little drunk tonight; the guest of honour who lights the first lantern.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To finish the boundary survey by Monday and get home.

npcsInvolved.name: Santiago "Santi" Rivera, 25
npcsInvolved.description: Quiet, wiry, an Army medic in 1971 and 1972, a community-college student in Bethlehem on the GI Bill; eats like a soldier and watches the doors.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Get the survey done, get paid, get back to classes Tuesday.

npcsInvolved.name: Roscoe Talmadge, 50
npcsInvolved.role: District game protector, Pennsylvania Game Commission (a companion)
npcsInvolved.description: Lean, green uniform jacket, a slow smile, a Game Commission truck and a shotgun in it; here about a young bear in the garbage cans.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Pie, and to see the bear doesn't get into trouble.

npcsInvolved.name: Marvin Eckhart, 64
npcsInvolved.description: Bow tie, a silver pompadour, a gin and tonic on the piano lid, knows every song from every revue. Wrote the 1958 'Lantern Lake Waltz'.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To play every song once more for people who remember them.

npcsInvolved.name: Bev Kleinfelter, 55
npcsInvolved.role: Arts and crafts counselor, 1949 to 1971; slide show; the witness
npcsInvolved.description: Silver braid, paint under her nails, brisk and kind; repainted the Lantern Night masks in 1958; saw the masked man on Thursday.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To get the slide show right, and not to remember 1962.

rewards.money: Nothing changes hands tonight but hospitality: the rooms and meals are on Pinecrest ("Miss Delamater's rule: the staff never pays"), the Honor System bar is fifty cents a drink, and Paula's Polaroid film is seven dollars a pack of ten. Gene Marcotte, if anyone helps him carry the survey stakes up from the truck, stands a round.
items: A carved Lantern Night mask, from Alvin's hands (CLUE A1; it works, Rites That Work Here)
Paula's Lantern Night Polaroids, one with a grey faceless shape on the dock ladder (CLUE B5)
The memory of the 1962 slide and the photo wall (CLUE D2)
Bev Kleinfelter's statement in Nolan's notebook
A paper lantern and a cedar shingle, unused

twists: Coach is genuinely kind tonight, and the players should like him. He remembers everyone's drink, he makes Marvin play the old songs, he hugs Odessa twice. He also needs a face for the lake, and he chose the guest of honour for it before Gene had finished shaking his hand. Both are true.

Alvin's mask, pushed into a player's hands, is the first real protection in the campaign, and the players do not yet know it. If the player wears it on the dock, Old Glass cannot borrow their face (Rule One), and the GM should quietly note it.

The man on the spillway is not stalking the party. He is guarding the dam, the Outlet and the bridge beyond it, because nothing the lake takes can leave without crossing them. Everything he does all weekend makes sense from that one idea, and almost none of it makes sense without it.

Old Glass, wearing Gene's face for the first time, is not menacing; it is curious, and lost. It came up the ladder to look at the warm lit windows. Nell's 'Curtis, Curtis' at the glass is the first time in fifteen years anyone has said its name near the water, and it does not know why it went back down.
dmTips: Before the first scene, ask the players what they do not want in the game, and honour 'skip that' at any time (dread.json running_horror). Mention, without spoiling, that this campaign involves deep water, being shut in, and a killing that happens off-screen.
Pinecrest was always for grown-ups. If a player asks about young guests, the answer is the 1934 brochure on the Lodge wall: eighteen years and over. Nobody in this campaign is a child, ever.

Spend real time on supper and the slide show. The campaign works only if the players care about Winnie, Opal, Marvin, Bev and Gene before Saturday morning, and if Coach is the warmest person in the room.

At the lanterns, ask each player directly: does your character look down into the water? For how long? Masked or not? Write it down. These are the faces Old Glass has seen, and you will need them on Saturday night.

The man on the spillway should be a straight slasher beat: still, silent, gone. Let the players chase him and lose him. Do not let them catch him tonight; he knows the Neck and they do not (Always Ahead).
Paula's Polaroid of the ladder should look like a flaw on the film tonight. Do not insist on its meaning; tomorrow, after the body, it will land on its own.

Two Genes is the scene that ends the night. Play it through the window, in reflection, so the player sees both men at once. Stop there: no attack, no chase, just Gene on the porch in the rain asking who the joker is.
Budget about an hour for arrival and supper, an hour for the slide show and the mask box, and an hour for Lantern Night and the double.
